items.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effects of different exercise modalities on frailty in older adults.
items.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To synthesize randomized evidence on unimodal resistance exercise, walking, and Tai Chi for frailty in older adults and to explore whether intervention characteristics may help explain between-study heterogeneity. Unlike broader reviews of multicomponent or non-pharmacological interventions, this review focuses on these three standalone modalities and reports modality- and dose-characteristic subgroup estimates.
METHODS: This systematic review and meta-analysis followed PRISMA 2020 and was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251179862). Five databases were searched from inception to October 2025. Two reviewers independently screened records, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias with the Cochrane tool. Standardized mean differences (SMDs) were pooled using inverse-variance models; random-effects models were used when substantial heterogeneity was present. Prespecified subgroup analyses examined exercise modality and intervention characteristics. Leave-one-comparison-out sensitivity analysis was used to assess influence. Funnel-plot findings were considered exploratory because few comparisons were available.
RESULTS: Ten articles contributed 13 eligible exercise-control comparisons comprising 1,361 participant observations (682 intervention and 679 control). The overall random-effects estimate favored exercise (SMD = -0.57, 95% CI -0.91 to -0.24), but heterogeneity was substantial (I 2 = 88%) and the approximate 95% prediction interval crossed the null (-1.73 to 0.57). Resistance-exercise comparisons showed a significant pooled association with lower frailty scores (SMD = -0.78, 95% CI -1.22 to -0.35), whereas walking and Tai Chi estimates were imprecise and not statistically significant. Leave-one-comparison-out estimates remained in the same direction (SMD range, -0.65 to -0.46), although heterogeneity remained high. Dose-characteristic subgroup findings were based on small numbers of comparisons and should be regarded as exploratory rather than as evidence of an optimal prescription.
CONCLUSION: Resistance-exercise trials showed a significant pooled reduction in frailty scores, but the available evidence does not establish superiority over walking or Tai Chi because no direct head-to-head or network comparison was performed. High heterogeneity, imprecise modality subgroups, and sparse dose strata limit certainty. The dose-related findings should be used to generate hypotheses for adequately powered comparative trials rather than to prescribe an optimal regimen.

items.title: Effects of school-based physical activity interventions on physical fitness and psychosocial adaptation in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: School-based physical activity (PA) interventions are a population-level strategy for improving children's health, yet evidence on their combined effects on physical fitness and psychosocial adaptation remains fragmented. This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized evidence from controlled intervention trials (randomized and non-randomized) examining school-based PA interventions on physical fitness (cardiorespiratory fitness, muscular fitness, body composition) and psychosocial adaptation (self-esteem, psychological well-being, social functioning) in children aged 6-12 years.
METHODS: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, SPORTDiscus, Cochrane Library, and PsycINFO from inception to 15 January 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomized controlled trials with a minimum 8-week school-based PA intervention and at least one physical fitness or psychosocial outcome were eligible. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed using Hedges' g. Heterogeneity was assessed with I2 and Cochran's Q. Risk of bias was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool for RCTs and ROBINS-I for non-randomized trials.
RESULTS: Forty studies (39 randomized, 1 non-randomized) involving 21,793 participants met inclusion criteria. School-based PA interventions were associated with significant improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness (g = 0.36, 95% CI [0.25, 0.46], p < 0.001, I2 = 98%) and muscular fitness (g = 0.24, 95% CI [0.17, 0.31], p < 0.001, I2 = 93%); the small reduction in body mass index did not reach statistical significance (g = -0.11, 95% CI [-0.27, 0.04], p = 0.154, I2 = 98%). For psychosocial outcomes, significant small effects were found for self-esteem (g = 0.18, 95% CI [0.10, 0.27], p < 0.001), psychological well-being (g = 0.15, 95% CI [0.09, 0.21], p < 0.001), and social functioning (g = 0.21, 95% CI [0.04, 0.38], p = 0.018). Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested that larger effects were associated with multicomponent interventions, durations of ≥24 weeks, and ≥3 sessions per week.
CONCLUSION: School-based PA interventions were associated with small-to-moderate improvements in physical fitness and small improvements in psychosocial adaptation in children. The findings support integrating comprehensive PA programs into school curricula. However, the small effect sizes for psychosocial outcomes and substantial heterogeneity underscore the need for rigorous studies with standardized measurement protocols.

items.title: CagriSema versus Semaglutide 2.4 mg monotherapy for weight management in adults with overweight or obesity, with or without type 2 diabetes: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and trial sequential analysis.
items.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Semaglutide 2.4 mg is the reference pharmacotherapy for weight management, yet many patients do not reach ambitious weight-loss targets. CagriSema, a fixed-dose combination of cagrilintide and semaglutide, may offer additional benefit through complementary mechanisms. We quantified its incremental efficacy and safety against semaglutide 2.4 mg monotherapy in adults with overweight or obesity, with and without type 2 diabetes.
METHODS: This PRISMA 2020-compliant review (PROSPERO CRD420261380458) searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, ScienceDirect, ClinicalTrials.gov and WHO ICTRP to 30 June 2026 for randomised controlled trials comparing CagriSema with semaglutide 2.4 mg or placebo. Effects were pooled within two prespecified comparator strata using random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation of τ² and a Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman small-sample adjustment, with prediction intervals, leave-one-out and phase-3a-restricted sensitivity analyses, trial sequential analysis.
RESULTS: Five trials (4,746 unique participants) were included. Versus semaglutide 2.4 mg, CagriSema produced greater weight loss (mean difference -6.89 percentage points, 95% CI -8.70 to -5.06; I² = 33%; prediction interval -8.91 to -4.86), a greater absolute reduction in body weight (-7.16 kg, 95% CI -9.15 to -5.17) and in body-mass index (-2.41 kg/m², 95% CI -2.83 to -1.99), and roughly twice the likelihood of reaching a 20% reduction (RR 2.10, 95% CI 1.78 to 2.47). Waist circumference fell further (-4.07 cm, 95% CI -5.10 to -3.04). No incremental glycaemic benefit was detected, with intervals for glycated haemoglobin (-0.07, 95% CI -0.14 to 0.01) and fasting plasma glucose lying entirely within prespecified minimal important differences. Injection-site reactions were more frequent (RR 3.14, 95% CI 1.42 to 6.96); gastrointestinal adverse events were not significantly increased under the primary model (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.21).
CONCLUSION: CagriSema produces clinically meaningful additional weight loss and modest improvements in surrogate cardiometabolic measures compared with semaglutide 2.4 mg alone, at the cost of more frequent injection-site reactions and, at most, modestly more frequent gastrointestinal events. The evidence is insufficient to determine whether serious adverse events or neoplasms differ between treatments, and long-term durability, cardiovascular outcomes and body composition remain undetermined.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/, identifier CRD420261380458.

items.title: The Effects of Combined Caffeine and Sodium Bicarbonate Supplementation on Exercise Performance, Physiological Responses, and Gastrointestinal Tolerability: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
items.abstract: Background: Caffeine and sodium bicarbonate can individually enhance exercise performance, but whether their combined use provides additional benefits and how it affects physiological responses and gastrointestinal (GI) tolerability remain unclear. Objective: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effects of combined caffeine and sodium bicarbonate (CAF + SB) supplementation on exercise performance, physiological responses, and GI tolerability, and to determine whether it provides additional benefits compared with placebo or either supplement alone. Methods: PubMed, Web of Science, and SPORTDiscus were systematically searched from inception to 18 July 2026. Continuous outcomes were pooled using random-effects models and expressed as mean differences (MDs) or ratios of means (RoMs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), as appropriate. Within-participant correlations in crossover trials were accounted for, and robustness was examined using leave-one-out analyses and alternative correlation coefficients. Rating of perceived exertion (RPE) and GI symptoms were synthesized narratively. Results: Thirteen crossover trials were included. Compared with placebo, CAF + SB supplementation increased mean power (MD = 8.43 W, 95% CI = 1.85 to 15.00, p = 0.012) and reduced time-trial completion time (RoM = 0.984, 95% CI = 0.970 to 0.998, p = 0.022), corresponding to an estimated reduction of 1.6%. However, both findings were sensitive to the exclusion of individual studies in leave-one-out analyses, indicating limited robustness. CAF + SB did not significantly improve mean power compared with caffeine or sodium bicarbonate alone. Compared with placebo, CAF + SB increased blood HCO3- and post-exercise lactate concentrations, although the HCO3- evidence was limited by heterogeneity or few studies. Narrative findings showed no consistent effect on RPE or GI tolerability. Conclusions: CAF + SB supplementation may produce modest improvements in selected exercise-performance outcomes compared with placebo, but these findings are not robust because their statistical significance depends on individual studies. Current evidence does not establish an additional performance benefit over caffeine or sodium bicarbonate alone. The observed physiological responses do not, by themselves, demonstrate superior performance, and the gastrointestinal tolerability of CAF + SB remains uncertain.

items.title: Time-restricted feeding with resistance training is not superior to conventional feeding for body composition and muscle strength: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract: Intermittent fasting is becoming popular for its quick benefits on body composition. With rising interest in weight loss, understanding its impact on fat-free mass is essential. It investigates the effects of time-restricted feeding compared to conventional diets on body composition in healthy adults undergoing resistance training. The registration is in PROSPERO (CRD42023423274), and ethical approval was not required. No financial support was received. Databases consulted included MEDLINE, CENTRAL, Embase, and Scopus, with the final search conducted on November 13, 2023. Only randomized controlled trials with healthy human participants aged 18 or older, who underwent TRF and strength training, were included. The risk of bias was assessed using the RoB2 tool. The review comprises 5 studies, with a final sample of 120 individuals. Among them, only 2 studies showed a statistically significant difference in the impact of fasting on body weight and fat mass. Regarding fat-free mass, it remained consistent across groups at the intervention's end. The meta-analysis suggested an estimate of -0.48kg (95% CI: -2.52 to 1.56), indicating that the average result did not significantly differ from zero. Contrary to the initial hypothesis, the findings do not provide statistically significant evidence that TRF increases fat-free mass.
items.journal: Anais da Academia Brasileira de Ciencias

items.title: Impact of body composition on clinical outcomes in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Abnormalities in body composition are common in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC); however, their impact across different treatment modalities remains poorly understood. We systematically reviewed the prognostic value of body composition in patients with HCC, stratified by curative, locoregional, and systemic therapies.
METHODS: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science (January 2015-March 2025) for studies reporting associations between CT/MRI or bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA)-assessed body composition and outcomes in HCC.
RESULTS: Ninety-two studies were included (35 curative, 10 locoregional, 39 systemic, 8 mixed). Sarcopenia prevalence ranged from 6.4% to 62.8% (median study-level prevalence 38%-50% depending on treatment stratum). Sarcopenia independently predicted worse overall survival across all strata: curative (HR 1.52-3.76), locoregional (HR 1.72-2.51), and systemic therapies (HR 1.34-2.20). Sarcopenic obesity conferred the highest risk in the curative setting (HR up to 3.15). In systemic therapy, myosteatosis independently predicted mortality (HR 1.45-2.01), whereas visceral adiposity was protective (HR 0.56-0.66). In a random-effects meta-analysis of 44 studies, sarcopenia was associated with a pooled HR of 1.85 (95% CI 1.75-1.94; I2=0%), with consistent effects across curative (HR 1.86), locoregional (HR 2.10), and systemic strata (HR 1.71). Sarcopenia also predicted recurrence after curative treatment (pooled HR 1.71, 95% CI 1.61-1.82; k=14).
CONCLUSIONS: Sarcopenia predicts mortality in HCC, independently of treatment modality. Visceral adiposity appears detrimental after curative treatment but may be paradoxically protective during systemic therapy. Body composition should be integrated into clinical decision-making in HCC, though a clear consensus on measurement standardization is needed.

items.title: Comparative effectiveness of telerehabilitation vs. face-to-face rehabilitation in adults with chronic low back pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic low back pain (CLBP) is a major cause of disability worldwide and creates substantial rehabilitation demand. When core rehabilitation content is similar, the comparative effectiveness of telerehabilitation (TR) and face-to-face rehabilitation as delivery modes remains unclear.
METHODS: Methods: This meta-analysis used strict eligibility criteria to distinguish the two delivery pathways and better isolate delivery-mode effects. PubMed, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, and Embase were searched for randomized controlled trials in adults with CLBP. Paper-based home exercise programs, continuous hybrid delivery, and remote-assessment-only designs were excluded. Random-effects meta-analyses used standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). RoB 2 and GRADE assessed risk of bias and evidence certainty. Sensitivity and subgroup analyses were conducted.
RESULTS: Ten trials involving 562 participants were included. Content-matched primary analyses found no significant difference between TR and face-to-face rehabilitation in pain intensity (7 trials; SMD = -0.05, 95% CI - 0.34 to 0.24; very low certainty) or functional disability (8 trials; SMD = 0.22, 95% CI - 0.07 to 0.52; low certainty). In secondary analyses including two trials that provided manual therapy only to the face-to-face group, pain intensity did not differ significantly (9 trials; SMD = -0.01, 95% CI - 0.26 to 0.24), whereas functional disability favored face-to-face rehabilitation (10 trials; SMD = 0.26, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.52). Subgroup interaction tests were nonsignificant for intervention duration, weekly treatment frequency, and supervision status.
CONCLUSION: When rehabilitation content was similar, TR and face-to-face rehabilitation showed no statistically significant differences in pain intensity or functional disability. However, these findings should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalent effectiveness between TR and face-to-face rehabilitation, because the certainty of evidence was low for functional disability and very low for pain intensity, and the functional disability estimate was sensitive to the exclusion of one study. Future high-quality trials with comparable interventions and longer follow-up are needed, particularly direct comparisons of supervised and unsupervised TR.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: PROSPERO, CRD420261467122.

items.title: Impact of different protein sources on acute muscle protein synthesis following resistance training: a systematic review with standard and dose-response network meta-analyses.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The combination of protein intake and resistance training (RT) plays a pivotal role in stimulating muscle protein synthesis (MPS), yet the impact of different protein sources remains an area of active investigation. Therefore, a systematic review incorporating standard and dose‒response network meta-analyses was performed.
METHODS: Systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, EBSCOhost (including MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus, CINAHL), and Scopus. Eligible studies included healthy adults (≥18 years) who were undergoing acute resistance exercise followed by a single protein bolus (any type or dose, except blends or enriched with anabolic agents). Muscle biopsies were required before and after RT/protein intake without additional food in between. Trials measuring hourly MPS rates via tracer techniques were included (n = 51).
RESULTS: In the standard network meta-analysis (NMA), native whey (P-score = 0.81, MD = 0.05% [0.00; 0.10]), pea protein (0.77, MD = 0.05% [-0.02; 0.11]), whole egg protein (0.72, MD = 0.04% [-0.01; 0.09]), mycoprotein (0.66, MD = 0.03% [-0.02; 0.08]), and whey protein (0.58, MD = 0.02% [0.01; 0.04]) ranked highest for estimated efficacy in stimulating post-RT hourly MPS (in descending order) (only whey protein showed a statistically significant effect) with low to moderate certainty of evidence. Dose‒response NMA revealed that certain animal- (native whey and whole egg protein) and plant- (pea and mycoprotein) based protein sources to show the highest predicted MPS responses with doses of 18-25 g.
CONCLUSIONS: Animal- (native whey, whey, whole egg) and plant-based (pea, mycoprotein) proteins ranked similarly for estimated acute MPS stimulation when combined with RT; however, only whey protein showed a statistically significant effect, and protein sources represented by few studies should be interpreted with caution.
items.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

items.title: Behavior plan and the intention-behavior gap in physical activity among adolescents and college students: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: (1) To conduct a meta-analysis on the structure of the TPB extended model to examine the predictive effects of its components on physical activity participation among adolescents and college students; (2) To investigate the moderating effects of key research dimensions, including participant groups, cultural backgrounds, physical activity measurement methods, study designs, and gender composition (proportion of females), on the relationships between variables in the TPB extended model and behavioral models for adolescents and college students physical activity; (3) To test the mediating effects of the TPB extended model; (4) To examine the direct effect of perceived behavioral control on adolescents' and college students' behavior.
METHODS: A systematic literature search was conducted across multiple databases to identify studies applying the extended Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) model to physical activity (PA) in adolescents and college students (approximately 10-24 years). A total of 28 articles (including 31 independent samples, with a total of 19,652 unique participants) met the inclusion criteria. Pairwise meta-analyses were performed using random-effects models in CMA 3.0 software. Meta-analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM) was conducted in Amos 24.0, with covariance matrix and harmonic mean constructed based on the summarized correlation matrix. Moderation analyses were conducted to examine the moderating effects of participant group, cultural background, physical activity measurement method, study design, and gender composition. Publication bias was assessed using funnel plots and Egger's regression tests, and methodological quality was evaluated using the adapted Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS-xs).
RESULTS: The TPB extended model explained 54.7% of intention differences, 29.2% of behavior differences, and 28.9% of behavior plan differences. Behavioral intention was found to be a significant statistical mediator variable connecting the three major factors of TPB with behavior, and additional indirect effects have been observed through the sequential pathway of behavioral intention and behavior plan. Moderator analyses revealed that the strength of several TPB relationships was contingent upon participant characteristics (adolescents and college students), cultural background, measurement methods, and study design.
CONCLUSION: The TPB extended model demonstrates predictive utility for adolescents and college student's physical activities at the aggregate level and can explain, on average, substantial variations in behavioral intention, behavior, and behavior plan across the diverse studies synthesized here. Nevertheless, the extreme heterogeneity (I 2 > 90% for many pairwise associations) indicates that effect sizes vary considerably across populations, instruments, and study designs, limiting the generalizability of any single pooled estimate to specific subgroups or settings. In this cross-sectional synthesis, Perceived Behavioral Control (PBC) showed the strongest statistical association with behavioral intention. Behavior plan was also statistically associated with the relationship between behavioral intention and action, and may represent a potential explanatory pathway; however, the predominantly cross-sectional design precludes any causal or temporal inferences. The action path of this model is moderated by participant group, cultural background, measurement method, and study design, highlighting its contextual sensitivity. These findings underscore that PBC and behavior plan may be key variables for inclusion in future intervention designs, although their causal impact on behavior change still remains to be established via controlled trials.

items.title: Vices and vegetables: a systematic review and series of meta-analyses examining the relationships among compensatory health beliefs with health-related intentions and behaviors.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Compensatory health beliefs (CHBs), the belief that a healthy behavior can offset the effects of a health-compromising one, have been theorized to both justify unhealthy behaviors and motivate health-promoting ones. However, findings in the literature are inconsistent.
METHODS: These meta-analyses synthesized 252 effect sizes from 59 independent samples using robust variance estimation to examine the relationships between CHBs and four outcomes: intentions and engagement in compensatory health behaviors and intentions and engagement in health-compromising behaviors.
RESULTS: Approximately 13,760 individuals were represented across these analyses (ages 12-79; women ∼66.1%; college-based = 69.8%). CHBs were significantly associated with greater intentions to engage in compensatory health behaviors (r = 0.21) and with greater engagement in health-compromising behaviors (r = 0.18), but were not reliably associated with compensatory health behaviors or intentions to engage in health-compromising behaviors. Heterogeneity was substantial across all models, but only one significant moderator emerged: CHBs were more strongly associated with compensatory intentions in studies examining diet compared to physical activity. Funnel plot symmetry and stability across values of ρ supported the robustness of findings.
CONCLUSIONS: These results highlight the potential for CHBs to undermine health behavior change efforts, particularly when intentions to engage in healthy behaviors are not carried out. Future work should explore state-level CHBs and real-time decision-making to clarify how and when these beliefs influence behavior.
items.journal: Annals of behavioral medicine : a publication of the Society of Behavioral Medicine

items.title: Efficacy and safety of bone marrow aspirate and bone marrow aspirate concentrate in orthopedic conditions: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials.
items.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Bone marrow aspirate (BMA) and bone marrow aspirate concentrate (BMAC) have emerged as autologous orthobiologic strategies aimed at modulating inflammation and promoting tissue repair in orthopedic conditions. However, evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) remains heterogeneous, and their clinical role relative to established treatments is still debated. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the efficacy, structural effects, and safety of BMA and BMAC in adults with orthopedic conditions based exclusively on RCT evidence.
METHODS: A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from December 2015 to December 2025. Eligible studies were RCTs comparing BMA or BMAC with placebo, conventional injective therapies, exercise therapy, or standard surgical procedures. Outcomes included pain, functional performance, imaging-based structural healing, treatment failure or revision, and safety. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2.0 tool, and results were synthesized narratively.
RESULTS: Twenty-one RCTs involving knee osteoarthritis, ACL injury or reconstruction, rotator cuff tears, focal cartilage defects, osteonecrosis, discogenic low back pain, and glenohumeral osteoarthritis were included. Across trials, BMA/BMAC was generally associated with improvements in pain and function, although superiority over comparators was inconsistent and depended on the clinical condition and treatment strategy.
DISCUSSION: Signals of greater benefit were observed in selected patients with early-stage knee osteoarthritis, focal cartilage pathology, nonsurgical ligament injuries, and rotator cuff disorders.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251241519, identifier CRD420251241519.

items.title: Dose-response relationships between temporal variables of blood flow restriction exercise and physiological adaptations: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: To evaluate dose-response relationships between temporal variables of blood flow restriction (BFR) exercise as a physiological stimulus and changes in physiological adaptations.
METHODS: Following PRISMA, Web of Science, PubMed, SPORTDiscus and Scopus were searched (inception-3 May 2026) for RCTs in athletes or physically active healthy adolescents and young adults comparing BFR interventions with conventional exercise protocols. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 and certainty with GRADE. In total, 15 articles (16 trials; 50 effect sizes) were included. Standardised mean differences (SMDs) were computed, with effect directions harmonised for context-dependent outcomes (HR, RER, RPE) so that positive values consistently reflect physiological improvements. These SMDs were pooled using a three-level random-effects model with robust variance estimation (RVE; clustered by study). A DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model with inverse-variance weighting was used for consistency checks.
RESULTS: Overall, BFR exercise elicited significant physiological adaptations (SMD = 0.249, 95% CI: 0.095-0.405), with findings remaining consistent in the DerSimonian-Laird model (overall SMD = 0.231, 95% CI: 0.111-0.349). By intensity, effects were: high-intensity BFR group (SMD = 0.208, 95% CI: 0.163-0.252), moderate-intensity group (SMD = 0.315, 95% CI: -0.465-1.095) and low-intensity group (SMD = 0.293, 95% CI: 0.057-0.529). Meta-regression showed positive associations of effect size with BFR duration (β = 0.0136, p = 0.0011) and stimulus duration (β = 0.0104, p = 0.0347). However, after adjusting for the period, BFR duration was not significant (p = 0.0972) due to collinearity; BFR pressure was not a significant moderator. Regarding specific physiological responses, only VO2max showed robust statistical significance (SMD = 0.386, 95% CI: 0.055-0.717).
CONCLUSION: The most consistent evidence for BFR-induced improvements relates specifically to VO2max, whereas effects on other physiological outcomes remain tentative. In the initial RVE, among the specific physiological outcomes, VO2max, MPO, and RER reached significance, whereas HR and MAP were borderline; upon DL re-verification, only VO2max retained significance. Low-intensity BFR showed clearer advantages over conventional low-intensity exercise, whereas benefits were smaller versus conventional high-intensity protocols. Both BFR duration and stimulus duration showed positive dose-response relationships with effect size. However, multivariable models revealed that the apparent effect of BFR duration was confounded by the total intervention period. In addition, no other variables exhibited significant moderating effects.

items.title: AI-Driven Lifestyle Interventions for Reducing Diabetes Risk: Systematic Review.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven lifestyle interventions are increasingly used for reducing diabetes risk. However, whether they produce clinical benefit beyond standard Diabetes Prevention Programs (DPPs) and whether effects vary by AI type, population, or delivery setting, remains uncertain.
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the effects of AI-driven lifestyle interventions on clinical, behavioral, and engagement outcomes among people with prediabetes or elevated diabetes risk and to assess whether effects differed by AI type, population, or delivery setting.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ClinicalTrials.gov, and citation searches were completed on August 3, 2026, for English-language reports published from 2015. Eligible studies evaluated AI-driven digital lifestyle interventions among people with prediabetes or elevated diabetes risks, or healthy participants in feasibility studies. One reviewer (OIE) screened records and extracted data; a second reviewer (TN) independently verified exclusions and extraction. Study quality was assessed with National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute tools appropriate to each design. Given substantial heterogeneity in designs, estimands, and outcome metrics, findings were synthesized narratively following the Synthesis Without Meta-Analysis guideline rather than pooled statistically.
RESULTS: Of 8032 records, 11 studies were included: 1 randomized, 1 nonrandomized comparative, 4 observational, and 5 uncontrolled pre-post studies. Seven evaluated AI lifestyle coaching systems, 2 predictive AI platforms, and 2 conversational AI chatbots. Ten of 11 studies used commercially developed platforms. Study quality was rated good for 5 studies, fair for 3, and poor for 3. The randomized controlled trial showed noninferiority of an AI-DPP versus human coach-led DPP for the combined 12-month outcome (23/183, 12.6% vs 23/185, 12.4%; risk difference 0.1%, 1-sided 95% CI -5.5%). Program initiation (171/183, 93.4% vs 153/185, 82.7%; risk difference 10.7%, 95% CI 4.2%-17.3%) and completion (117/183, 63.9% vs 93/185, 50.3%; risk difference 13.7%; 95% CI 3.6%-23.7%) were higher with AI, but this did not translate into superior clinical outcomes. The nonrandomized comparison found no advantage of AI-personalized messaging over static messaging in terms of BMI or physical activity. The remaining studies reported uncontrolled changes precluding causal inference. Evidence was insufficient to determine whether effects differed by population or delivery setting.
CONCLUSIONS: One randomized trial supports noninferiority, not superiority, of a specific AI-driven DPP relative to human coaching; the remaining evidence was nonrandomized, predominantly commercially developed, and hypothesis-generating. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic review to stratify evidence on AI-driven diabetes prevention by AI mechanism-coaching, predictive, and conversational-and by outcome domain, extending prior scoping work that mapped apps without appraising study quality or comparative effectiveness. This structured mapping shows where evidence is the strongest (engagement and weight) and the weakest (glycemic causality and generalizability), giving health systems a concrete basis for deciding where AI-DPP tools may supplement, rather than replace, standard DPP delivery, pending independent, adequately powered randomized trials.

items.title: Short-term Rhodiola rosea supplementation improves premenstrual symptoms, reaction time, and perceived exertion in female taekwondo athletes: a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Premenstrual symptoms may negatively influence psychological readiness, cognitive-motor performance, and perceived exertion in female athletes. Rhodiola rosea (RR) is an adaptogenic herb that has been investigated for its potential effects on fatigue, stress tolerance, mood, and exercise-related outcomes. However, its effects on premenstrual symptoms and performance-related responses in female athletes remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the effects of short-term RR supplementation during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase on premenstrual symptoms, peripheral serum serotonin and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) concentrations, reaction time, perceived exertion, and aerobic performance-related indices in female taekwondo athletes with premenstrual syndrome (PMS).
METHODS: In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 24 female taekwondo athletes with moderate-to-severe PMS symptoms were randomly assigned to receive either 500 mg/day of standardised RR extract (n = 12) or placebo (n = 12) for 10 days during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase. Premenstrual symptoms were assessed using the Premenstrual Symptoms Screening Tool (PSST). Visual reaction time, peripheral serum serotonin and GABA concentrations, time to exhaustion (TTE), estimated VO₂max, and rating of perceived exertion (RPE) were evaluated before and after the intervention. Data were analysed using analysis of covariance with baseline values as covariates.
RESULTS: Compared with placebo, RR supplementation significantly reduced several PMS symptoms, including irritability, depression, anxiety, social withdrawal, decreased concentration, hypersomnia, food cravings, crying, skin problems, and abdominal pain (p < 0.05). The RR group demonstrated faster reaction time compared with placebo (adjusted mean difference: -60 ms; p < 0.001). Peripheral serum serotonin and GABA concentrations were significantly higher in the RR group than in the placebo group (p < 0.001). In addition, RR supplementation reduced post-exercise RPE (adjusted mean difference: -1.40 Borg units; p = 0.006). However, no significant differences were observed between groups in TTE or estimated VO₂max (p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: Short-term RR supplementation during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase may improve selected PMS symptoms, visual reaction time, and perceived exertion in female taekwondo athletes with PMS. Larger trials with hormonal confirmation of menstrual cycle phase, longer intervention periods, direct physiological measurements, and sport-specific performance assessments are required to confirm these findings.
items.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

items.title: GLP-1-Based therapies for obesity-related heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: an umbrella review incorporating broader heart failure and cardiometabolic evidence.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The cardiometabolic phenotype of obesity-related heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is increasing in clinical prevalence. Existing systematic reviews and meta-analyses have primarily summarized efficacy estimates for glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)-based therapies, but the credibility and independence of these syntheses remain uncertain because methodological limitations and overlap in primary trials have not been systematically evaluated. This umbrella review therefore appraised the methodological quality, overlap, consistency, and robustness of the existing review-level evidence rather than generating another efficacy synthesis.
METHODS: We conducted an umbrella review of systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and network meta-analyses evaluating GLP-1-based regimens in obesity-related HFpEF and adjacent cardiometabolic populations. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched over the preceding decade. The systematic review or meta-analysis was the unit of analysis. Methodological quality was assessed with AMSTAR 2, and overlap of primary studies across reviews was quantified using the corrected covered area (CCA). No de novo meta-analysis was performed; primary trials were examined only to assess overlap and calculate the CCA. Review-level findings were synthesized according to effect direction, consistency, precision, sample size, methodological quality, clinical relevance, and overlap.
RESULTS: Seventeen systematic reviews underwent qualitative profiling, of which 11 reported quantitative estimates relevant to the core review-level synthesis. For heart failure hospitalization, the review by Diallo et al. reported HR 0.78 (95% CI 0.73-0.84; n = 25,440). For the composite of cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalization, Diallo et al. reported HR 0.84 (95% CI 0.78-0.89), Ahmed HM et al. reported HR 0.76 (95% CI 0.64-0.90), and Ahmed M et al. reported RR 0.73 (95% CI 0.57-0.93). Existing reviews also consistently suggested improvements in functional status. The review by Gera et al. reported OR 0.85 (95% CI 0.77-0.93; n = 85,373) for stroke, whereas findings for cardiovascular and all-cause mortality remained inconsistent. Evidence for major adverse cardiovascular events was limited; the review by Gonzales-Uribe et al. reported HR 0.71 (95% CI 0.60-0.86). AMSTAR 2 classified six reviews as having low overall methodological confidence and five as having critically low overall methodological confidence. The CCA was 13.2%, indicating high overlap. All HR, RR, and OR values were estimates reported by included reviews and were not recalculated or quantitatively combined in this umbrella review.
CONCLUSIONS: At the level of existing evidence syntheses, GLP-1-based therapies appear most consistently associated with fewer heart failure hospitalizations and improved functional capacity in obesity-related HFpEF. However, the review-level evidence does not establish a consistent mortality benefit or support GLP-1-based therapy as a universal mortality-modifying treatment for HFpEF. These agents are better interpreted as emerging metabolic-functional therapies whose apparent benefits must be considered in light of methodological limitations and high overlap among reviews.

items.title: Phase angle assessed by bioelectrical impedance analysis in patients with colorectal cancer: a systematic review.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Malnutrition, altered body composition, and sarcopenia are common among patients with colorectal cancer (CRC) and are associated with poor treatment tolerance and adverse clinical outcomes. PhA, derived from BIA, reflects cellular membrane integrity and body cell mass and has been increasingly investigated as a potential marker of nutritional status and prognosis in oncology. However, the clinical relevance of PhA in patients with CRC has not yet been systematically synthesized.
METHODS: This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched for observational studies published between January 2000 and October 2025 that assessed PhA in adult patients with CRC. Data extraction and risk-of-bias assessment using the AXIS tool were performed independently by two reviewers. Due to substantial heterogeneity in study design, outcome definitions, and PhA cut-off values, a narrative synthesis was conducted.
RESULTS: A total of 10 studies involving 1,439 patients were included. Lower PhA values were consistently associated with adverse clinical outcomes. Four studies reported significantly shorter overall or progression-free survival among patients with low PhA. Four studies demonstrated associations between low PhA and unfavorable short-term outcomes, including postoperative complications, prolonged hospital stay, cancer-related complications, and early chemotherapy-related toxicity. Several studies also reported positive associations between PhA and indicators of nutritional status, body composition, muscle mass, muscle strength, and hydration balance. One longitudinal study showed that postoperative increases in PhA were accompanied by improvements in body composition parameters and reduced early chemotherapy-related toxicity.
CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence indicates that BIA-derived phase angle is associated with nutritional status, body composition, treatment tolerance, and survival outcomes in patients with colorectal cancer. However, heterogeneity in measurement protocols and cut-off values limits direct clinical application. Standardized assessment methods and prospective studies are needed to establish CRC-specific reference values and to determine whether interventions that improve PhA can translate into improved clinical outcomes.

items.title: Effects of different exercise types on visceral adipose tissue and glycemic parameters in adults with stage 1 cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome, particularly at stage 1, is increasingly prevalent worldwide. Although exercise interventions are recognized as effective in reducing visceral adipose tissue (VAT) and improving glucose metabolism, their effects in adults with stage 1 CKM syndrome remain unclear. This study aimed to systematically analyze the effects of different exercise types on VAT, fasting blood glucose (FBG), and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) in adults with stage 1 CKM syndrome.
METHODS: We searched six bibliographic databases-China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), WanFang Database, VIP Database, Web of Science, Embase, and PubMed-from inception to 15 April 2026, using the PICOS framework. A frequentist random-effects Network Meta-Analyses was conducted using STATA 18.0 software to evaluate the effects of interventions on VAT, FBG and HbA1c. The effectiveness of various exercise intervention types was ranked by calculating the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA), and the risk of bias was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias (ROB 2.0) tool. This study protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261304633).
RESULTS: Thirty-seven randomized controlled trials involving 3483 participants were included. Compared with the control group, aerobic training significantly decreased VAT [standardized mean difference = -0.44, 95% confidence interval (CI): (-0.62, -0.26)], while mind-body exercise (MBE) significantly improved FBG [mean difference (MD) = -1.16 mmol/L, 95% CI: (-1.57, -0.75)] and HbA1c [MD = -0.35%, 95% CI: (-0.62, -0.07)]. Subgroup analysis revealed that high-intensity interval training with an intervention duration of ≤ 12 weeks (SUCRA = 67%) and aerobic training with a duration of >12 weeks (SUCRA = 94.9%) had the highest probability of being the most effective intervention for reducing VAT in included studies. In addition, mind-body exercise ranked highest for FBG improvement, though with limited certainty.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings provide evidence that different exercise types exert distinct benefits on metabolic health in adults with stage 1 CKM syndrome. In particular, aerobic training may be more effective than other exercise types in reducing VAT, while MBE may contribute to more benefits in improving FBG and HbA1c.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261304633, Identifier CRD420261304633.

items.title: Temperature-dependent effects of post-exercise cold-water immersion on recovery: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cold-water immersion (CWI) is widely used as a recovery intervention to facilitate post-exercise recovery; however, inconsistent conclusions remain regarding temperature-dependent effects. Therefore, this meta-analysis aimed to comprehensively examine the effects of CWI on post-exercise recovery, focusing on delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) and biochemical markers of muscle damage, including creatine kinase (CK) and myoglobin (Mb), and to quantitatively compare the effects across different water temperatures.
METHODS: This study was conducted as a systematic review and meta-analysis in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines. Relevant studies were identified through searches of the PubMed, Web of Science, SPORTDiscus and SCOPUS databases. Only studies employing a single-session CWI intervention were included, and a total of 52 studies met the inclusion criteria. Effect sizes were calculated using standardized mean differences (SMD), and subgroup analyses were performed to compare the effects of water temperatures of approximately 5 °C, 10 °C, and 15 °C. The review protocol was not prospectively registered, and temperature subgroup analyses should be considered exploratory.
RESULTS: The meta-analysis demonstrated that CWI produced statistically significant moderate-to-large effects on DOMS, CK, and Mb during the post-exercise recovery period (DOMS: SMD = - 0.81; CK: SMD = - 0.64; Mb: SMD = - 0.93; all p < 0.001). Subgroup analyses by water temperature showed numerically smaller reductions in DOMS at ≈5 °C (SMD = - 0.2) compared with ≈10 °C (SMD = - 0.8) and ≈15 °C (SMD = - 0.9); however, the difference between temperature subgroups was not statistically significant (p = 0.79). CK and Mb were significantly reduced across all temperature ranges, with no significant differences between temperature subgroups.
CONCLUSION: On average, CWI was associated with reductions in DOMS, CK, and Mb, although substantial heterogeneity and wide prediction intervals indicate that these effects may not be consistently reproduced across settings. Numerically larger reductions in DOMS were observed at approximately 10-15 °C than at ≈5 °C, but neither subgroup analysis nor meta-regression confirmed a temperature-dependent effect. No water-temperature range can currently be considered superior.
CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.
REVIEW REGISTRATION: Not prospectively registered.

items.title: Load and breath-hold: impact of 7-day creatine monohydrate loading on breath-hold exercise performance - a double-blind randomized controlled trial.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Creatine supplementation enhances anaerobic energy availability and buffering capacity; however, its impact on muscle work under voluntary breath-hold (BH) remains unexplored. BH exercise increases reliance on anaerobic ATP production and creates a metabolic environment in which phosphocreatine-derived ATP may be particularly valuable. The aim of this study was to determine whether creatine monohydrate loading improves BH exercise performance in trained BH divers.
METHODS: A double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study assessed the effects of a 7-day creatine monohydrate loading protocol (20 g/day) on performance outcomes and fatigue markers during BH exercise performed on a bicycle ergometer in 20 trained BH divers (18 males, 2 females; mean age 41.6 ± 8.6 years). The trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: NCT07233707) on 16th November 2025 under the title Load and Hold: Impact of 7-Day Creatine Monohydrate Loading on Breath-Hold Cycling Performance (BREATHE-C). Testing consisted of a brief warm-up followed by a maximal cycling trial performed on a single breath, during which participants aimed to cover the greatest possible distance. Following pre-supplementation testing, participants were randomly assigned to either the creatine monohydrate (CR) or the placebo (PL) group. Pre- and post-supplementation measurements included total work (TW), time to exhaustion (TTE), peripheral blood lactate accumulation (LA), mean partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO₂) in exhaled air following BH exercise, and ratings of perceived exertions for BH (RPE-BH) and muscle fatigue (RPE-MF). In addition, participants underwent dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry to assess changes in body composition.
RESULTS: Significant Time × Group interactions were observed for TW (p = 0.011), TTE (p = 0.028), and fat-free mass (p = 0.017), with greater changes observed following creatine supplementation compared to PL. Furthermore, there was a significant Time × Group interaction for LA (p = 0.003), with greater changes observed in the PL group compared to CR. No significant between-group differences were observed for pCO₂, RPE-BH, RPE-MF, fat mass, or total body mass.
CONCLUSIONS: Creatine enhanced performance, as reflected by increases in TW and TTE, without elevating RPE-BH, although a slight increase in RPE-MF was observed. LA was lower in the CR compared to PL group, despite greater performance improvements. Overall, creatine appears to enhance BH exercise performance in trained BH divers, suggesting a potentially effective ergogenic strategy for BH-related sports.
items.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

items.title: Values, preferences, and treatment burden for initiation of GLP-1 receptor agonists, SGLT-2 inhibitors, tirzepatide, and finerenone in adults with type 2 diabetes: systematic review.
items.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To summarise existing evidence regarding the values, preferences, and perceived treatment burden of adults with type 2 diabetes when considering initiation of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA), sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT-2i), finerenone, or tirzepatide.
DESIGN: Systematic review.
DATA SOURCES: Medline, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from database inception to 7 January 2025 (updating a previous systematic review that captured literature up to 23 May 2020).
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: Quantitative or qualitative studies were included if they reported patient reported values, preferences, or treatment burden among adults with type 2 diabetes and compared initiation of GLP-1 RA, SGLT-2i, tirzepatide, or finerenone with each other or with other glucose-lowering treatments.
DATA EXTRACTION AND SYNTHESIS: Paired reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADE. Findings were synthesised narratively.
RESULTS: Thirty four studies (15 656 patients) were included, 17 of which were new since the previous 2021 review (8360 patients). Of the newly included studies, 10 evaluated GLP-1 RA, seven evaluated SGLT-2i, and one evaluated tirzepatide; no studies evaluated finerenone (because several studies compared multiple drug classes, these categories are not mutually exclusive). Across comparisons, patients consistently reported glycaemic efficacy, cardiovascular risk reduction, and simplicity of administration as their priorities. Oral once-daily regimens and once-weekly injectable treatments with easy-to-use devices were generally preferred. Weight loss was valued but was typically secondary to glycaemic and cardiovascular benefits. SGLT-2i and GLP-1 RA were often preferred over dipeptidyl peptidase 4-inhibitors (DPP-4i), thiazolidinediones, and insulins, but no consistent preference emerged for SGLT-2i over GLP-1 RA. Tirzepatide was favoured over semaglutide in a single study, largely due to greater haemoglobin A1c reduction and lower hypoglycaemia risk. Certainty of evidence for all comparisons was low or very low certainty.
CONCLUSION: Adults with type 2 diabetes prioritise treatment effectiveness and convenience among glucose-lowering treatments. Current evidence does not support a clear preference between SGLT-2i and GLP-1 RA, and data for finerenone are absent. These findings underscore the importance of shared decision making informed by individual patient priorities.
PROSPERO REGISTRATION: CRD42023429170.

items.title: Effects of high-intensity resistance training within concurrent training programs on athletic performance in elite athletes: a systematic review.
items.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: This systematic review aimed to evaluate the effects of high-intensity resistance training (HIRT), operationally defined as resistance protocols utilizing loads ≥ 75% of one-repetition maximum (1RM), on athletic performance outcomes-including muscular strength, power, jumping performance, speed, preplanned change-of-direction (COD) speed, and endurance-among elite athletes.
METHODS: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic search was conducted in Web of Science, PubMed, Scopus and SPORTDiscus to identify studies that applied HIRT in elite athlete populations. Google Scholar was additionally utilized for forward and backward citation tracking. Twelve studies met the inclusion criteria and were assessed using the PEDro scale. Data on intervention characteristics, testing protocols, and performance outcomes were extracted and synthesized narratively.
RESULTS: HIRT interventions (range: 5-18 weeks) demonstrated significant improvements in maximal strength (e.g., squat and bench press 1RM) and neuromuscular power-related outcomes across the majority of studies. Improvements in sprint speed, sport-specific velocity, and preplanned COD speed were also observed, although evidence for COD performance was limited to a single study. Endurance-related outcomes, including time to exhaustion, movement economy, and selected time-trial measures, generally favored HIRT, with no clear evidence of detrimental effects on aerobic-capacity-related outcomes. However, all included studies implemented HIRT within concurrent training programs rather than as an isolated intervention.
CONCLUSIONS: The available evidence suggests that HIRT may be an effective training component for improving strength, power, and selected performance outcomes in elite athletes when integrated into concurrent sport-specific training programs. The strongest support was observed for maximal strength and neuromuscular power, whereas evidence for preplanned COD speed remains preliminary and requires replication. Given the concurrent training designs, the absence of a formal GRADE assessment, and the generally small sample sizes, these findings should be interpreted as likely low-to-moderate certainty evidence rather than as proof of the isolated effects of HIRT. The review protocol was prospectively registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) on 6 January 2025 (Registration No.: CRD42025634254).

items.title: InBody bioelectrical impedance research in clinical nutrition: a bibliometric analysis of trends, applications, and evidence gaps, 2002-2025.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: InBody analyzers are widely used for body composition assessment in clinical nutrition research, but no platform-specific bibliometric study has mapped the development, dominant topics, or evidence gaps of the InBody literature. This study examined InBody-related research from 2002 to 2025.
METHODS: English-language original research articles were retrieved from the Science Citation Index Expanded within the Web of Science (WoS) Core Collection using the search term "InBody." Records were analyzed using Bibliometrix and VOSviewer. Analyses included descriptive bibliometrics, country and institutional productivity, journal productivity, citation impact, author-keyword co-occurrence, trend-topic analysis, and logistic growth modeling. Cross-database validation was conducted using Scopus and PubMed.
RESULTS: The final WoS corpus included 406 articles across 217 sources, with an annual growth rate of 19.7% and a mean of 17.7 citations per article; 294 articles (72.4%) were published from 2020 onward. South Korea contributed the largest fractional share (14.6%), while the United States produced the highest mean annual citation rate among the top 10 countries (4.93 citations/year). The logistic model fitted cumulative output closely (R2 = 0.97), with an estimated saturation ceiling of approximately 1,172 articles and a projected peak annual output of about 75 articles around 2028. The most-cited articles centered on validation against dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA). Author-keyword mapping identified seven clusters, including a clinically oriented cluster linking distinct but related themes of sarcopenia, older adults, phase angle, hemodialysis, malnutrition, and frailty. Recent trend topics included phase angle, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, frailty, young adults, and weight loss. Cross-database validation showed broadly consistent temporal, geographic, and source patterns across WoS, Scopus, and PubMed; all 12 leading WoS author keywords also appeared in Scopus, of which nine ranked within the Scopus top 10.
CONCLUSION: InBody-related research is expanding rapidly and shifting from device validation toward clinical application, particularly in geriatric and clinical nutrition. Three priorities emerge: (i) device-model-specific and population-specific validation, particularly under-represented regions; (ii) population- and condition-specific phase-angle reference ranges; and (iii) longitudinal and intervention-responsive designs rather than additional cross-sectional DXA comparisons. Addressing these priorities may support more consistent, evidence-based interpretation of InBody-derived body composition measures in nutrition and clinical practice.

items.title: The effect of exercise snacks on cardiorespiratory fitness, body composition, metabolic health, and muscle strength in sedentary individuals: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to investigate the effects of exercise snacks (ES) on cardiorespiratory fitness, body composition, metabolic health, and muscle strength in sedentary individuals.
METHODS: From database inception to February 5, 2026, four international databases (PubMed, Web of Science, SciELO, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials) and one Chinese database (China National Knowledge Infrastructure) were searched. The GRADE approach was used to assess the certainty of evidence, while the Cochrane Risk of Bias tools (RoB 2) and Risk of Bias In Non-randomized Studies of Intervention (ROBINS-I) were applied to evaluate the quality of randomized controlled trials and non-randomized studies, respectively. The pooled effects of study outcomes were estimated using a random-effects model based on meta-analysis. Subgroup analyses and meta-regression were conducted to explore potential moderating variables.
RESULTS: A total of 22 studies involving 994 participants were included. The meta-analysis showed that ES significantly improved VO2max (Hedges' g = 1.24, 95% CI: 0.53 to 1.95, p < 0.001, I2 = 75.0%, τ2 = 1.13), VO2peak (Hedges' g = 0.63, 95% CI: 0.05 to 1.22, p < 0.05, I2 = 55.0%, τ2 = 0.19), triglycerides (Hedges' g = 1.05, 95% CI: 0.05 to 2.06, p < 0.05, I2 = 84.0%, τ2 = 0.65), and blood glucose (Hedges' g = -0.83, 95% CI: -1.51 to -0.15, p < 0.05, I2 = 78.0%, τ2 = 0.69) in sedentary populations. However, significant publication bias was detected for VO2max, and the trim-and-fill analysis yielded an adjusted effect estimate that was no longer statistically significant (Hedges' g = 0.62, 95% CI: -0.59 to 1.83, p = 0.32). No significant differences were observed in body fat, muscle mass, strength, or insulin levels.
CONCLUSION: As a short-duration, high-frequency intervention, ES may improve cardiorespiratory fitness and certain metabolic health indicators in sedentary individuals. However, the finding for VO2max should be interpreted cautiously because the trim-and-fill adjusted estimate was not statistically significant, suggesting that publication bias may have influenced the observed effect. It provides a potentially sustainable and effective exercise intervention strategy for sedentary individuals.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: PROSPERO (CRD420261347411).

items.title: Effectiveness of dynamic neuromuscular stabilization-based interventions for nonspecific low back pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Nonspecific low back pain (NLBP) is a leading cause of disability and imposes substantial public health and socioeconomic burdens. Dynamic Neuromuscular Stabilization (DNS) is increasingly used in NLBP rehabilitation, but quantitative evidence of its effects remains limited. We systematically reviewed and meta-analyzed controlled trials evaluating DNS-based interventions for NLBP.
METHODS: PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, the Cochrane Library, and CNKI were searched. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data. Random-effects meta-analysis, subgroup analyses, and leave-one-out analyses were performed using Review Manager 5.4 and Stata 17.0. Potential small-study effects were examined using Begg's rank-correlation test.
RESULTS: Eight studies involving 289 participants were included. The pooled analysis favored DNS-based interventions for pain-related outcomes (SMD = -1.17, 95% CI: -1.85 to -0.48), but heterogeneity was substantial (I2 = 85%). Subgroup analyses by intervention strategy, duration, weekly frequency, and session duration did not clearly account for the heterogeneity and were considered exploratory. Begg's test yielded p = 0.063, but the assessment of publication bias and small-study effects was inconclusive given the limited evidence base. Leave-one-out analysis indicated that no individual study alone materially altered the pooled estimate, but it did not resolve the remaining clinical and methodological uncertainties.
DISCUSSION: DNS-based interventions may reduce pain-related outcomes in individuals with NLBP; however, the magnitude, clinical importance, and generalizability of the effect remain uncertain. Adequately powered, high-quality RCTs using standardized DNS protocols, clearly defined comparators, and consistent pain-specific outcomes are needed.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, PROSPERO (No. CRD420251152728).

items.title: Effectiveness of exergaming interventions for adults with cancer: a systematic review.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Exergaming, which integrates physical exercise with interactive digital games, has gained attention as a supportive approach in cancer rehabilitation. However, uncertainty remains regarding its effects across different phases of cancer care and its feasibility in clinical and home-based settings. This systematic review synthesized evidence on the feasibility, safety, and effects of exergaming interventions among adults with cancer, with particular attention to interventions delivered during active treatment and after treatment completion.
METHODS: PubMed, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, Scopus, Embase, CINAHL, and SPORTDiscus were searched from inception to April 2025. Randomized and nonrandomized intervention studies evaluating exergaming among adults with cancer were included. Outcomes were synthesized narratively across physical, psychological, symptom-related, quality-of-life, biological or physiological, and feasibility domains.
RESULTS: Twenty-five publications representing 19 distinct study cohorts met the inclusion criteria. Interventions varied substantially in platform, setting, duration, and training dose, most commonly lasting 4-16 weeks with 2-5 sessions per week. Reported recruitment rates ranged from 11.8% to 85.7%, adherence from 62% to 100%, and attrition from 0% to 47.4%. No serious intervention-related adverse events were reported among studies that provided safety data, although adverse-event reporting was incomplete. Favorable findings were reported for physical activity, mobility, balance, upper-extremity function, fatigue, and selected psychological and quality-of-life outcomes. In contrast, findings for muscle strength, pain, body composition, and biological or physiological markers were inconsistent.
CONCLUSIONS: Exergaming appears to be a feasible and acceptable adjunct to cancer rehabilitation, with potential benefits for selected physical, symptom-related, and psychosocial outcomes. However, the evidence remains preliminary, and exergaming should be considered an adjunct rather than a replacement for conventional exercise or physiotherapy. Adequately powered randomized trials using standardized intervention protocols, consistent outcome reporting, longer follow-up, and more diverse cancer populations are needed.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/display_record.php?ID=CRD42024530181, identifier CRD42024530181.

items.title: Additive effects of active vitamin D3 or vitamin E administration on therapeutic lower-limb home exercise for knee osteoarthritis: A pilot prospective randomized controlled trial.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Quadriceps weakness, inflammation, and reduced physical function are common in knee osteoarthritis (OA), and lower limb exercise therapy is an established non-pharmacological treatment. Vitamin D3 (vit D3) and vitamin E (vit E) have been proposed as adjunctive therapies; however, clinical findings are inconsistent. We aimed to examine whether combining lower limb home exercises with oral active vit D3 or vit E supplementation provides additive benefits compared with home exercise alone in women with symptomatic knee OA.
METHODS: Eighty-eight postmenopausal women with knee OA (Kellgren-Lawrence grade 2-4; 71.9 ± 5.6 years) were randomly assigned to receive therapeutic lower limb home exercise only, home exercise with active vit D3 administration, or home exercise with vit E administration. Participants performed isometric lower limb exercises twice daily for 24 weeks. Subsequently, they were assessed using the Japanese knee osteoarthritis measure (JKOM) as the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes were short-form health survey, grip strength, quadriceps muscle strength, 10-m walk test, inflammatory markers, bone mineral density, and body composition. For data analyses, we used paired and independent t tests, analysis of variance, and analysis of covariance, adjusting for age, body mass index, and Kellgren-Lawrence grade.
RESULTS: Eighty participants completed follow-up. All groups showed significant improvements in JKOM score, quadriceps muscle strength, and 10-m walk test. Grip strength improved significantly only in the group that received active vit D. No significant between-group differences were observed in JKOM scores, short-form health survey-36, muscle strength, or physical performance. Inflammatory markers decreased significantly in the vit E group, although between-group differences were not observed. No other significant between-group differences were found, except in bone mineral density.
CONCLUSIONS: Administering active vit D3 or vit E for 24 weeks as an adjunct to lower limb home exercises did not yield significant additive effects on symptoms, muscle strength, or physical performance in women with knee OA. Exercise therapy alone remained effective, and vitamin supplementation showed nutrient-specific trends.

items.title: Preference for Resistance Training Volume After Acute Exercise in Women With Fibromyalgia: A Randomized Crossover Clinical Trial.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: To evaluate participants' preferences following acute exposure to three resistance training protocols differing solely in the number of sets performed.
METHODS: Randomized crossover clinical trial. Thirty-eight women aged 18-65 years with fibromyalgia diagnosed according to the 2016 American College of Rheumatology criteria completed the study. All participants were naïve to resistance training during the previous 6 months and completed every intervention protocol and assessment. Participants performed three resistance training sessions in randomized order, consisting of one-, two-, or three-set protocols separated by 7-day washout periods. Exercise selection, intensity, and repetitions were standardized across protocols, with the number of sets representing the only intervention variable. The primary outcome was participant preference for resistance training volume after completion of all three protocols. Secondary outcomes included treatment expectancy, pain intensity assessed before and after exercise and 24 hours later, and exercise execution time.
RESULTS: No participant selected the one-set protocol as the preferred training volume, whereas the two- and three-set protocols were equally preferred, each being selected by 50% of participants (p < 0.001; Cohen's w = 0.71). Treatment expectancy did not differ significantly among protocols (p = 0.20). No between-protocol differences in pain intensity were observed at any assessment time point. A significant within-protocol reduction in pain over time was identified only for the two-set protocol (p = 0.015); however, the magnitude of change did not reach the predefined minimal clinically important difference. Exercise execution time did not differ significantly among training volumes, and no serious adverse events occurred during the study.
DISCUSSION: Women with fibromyalgia demonstrated equivalent preference for resistance training protocols involving two and three sets, whereas no participant identified the one-set protocol as the preferred option. Treatment expectancy was similar across protocols, and no clinically meaningful differences in pain intensity were observed. These findings support the incorporation of patient preference into individualized resistance training prescriptions and warrant further investigation of whether such preferences translate into improved long-term adherence and clinical outcomes.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: NCT06424743, 2024-08-21).
items.journal: Physiotherapy research international : the journal for researchers and clinicians in physical therapy

items.title: The Effects of Multi-Strain Probiotic SLAB51 Intake on Aerobic Performance and Oxidative Stress Responses in Elite Athletes: A Randomized Crossover Trial.
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Exercise performance and recovery depend on interactions between energy metabolism and redox regulation. SLAB51, a multi-strain probiotic, may influence oxygen-related metabolism and antioxidant responses, but evidence in elite athletes remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of SLAB51 supplementation on aerobic exercise capacity and oxidative stress responses in elite athletes.
METHODS: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial evaluated the effects of SLAB51 supplementation on aerobic exercise performance and oxidative stress in elite athletes. Participants received SLAB51 and placebo for one week each, separated by a two-week washout period. Assessments were performed at baseline, after a single intake, and after one week of intake. Exercise performance was evaluated using a treadmill-based Bruce protocol, and physiological and oxidative stress markers were measured. Data were analyzed using two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA), supplemented by post hoc linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) accounting for the crossover design.
RESULTS: The original ANOVA showed significant treatment × time interactions for exercise duration, duration above a respiratory exchange ratio (RER) of 1.0, and pre-exercise superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity, but not for maximal oxygen uptake, lactate removal, or malondialdehyde concentration. The additional post hoc LMM analysis also identified a significant treatment difference in exercise duration after one week (mean difference = 33.32 s, 95% CI: 17.42-49.22, p < 0.001), with significant differences in duration above RER 1.0 and SOD activity also observed after one week.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings support the potential benefits of one-week SLAB51 supplementation for exercise duration in elite athletes, consistent with the additional crossover-adjusted analysis. Favorable differences in duration above RER 1.0 and pre-exercise antioxidant enzyme activity warrant further investigation.

items.title: Effects of Body-Mass-Scaled Protein and Leucine Supplementation on Body Composition and Cardiometabolic Blood Markers During Weight Loss in Older Men-A Randomized Controlled Trial.
items.abstract: Background: Overweight and obesity are burgeoning health epidemics. Diets including alternate-day fasting (ADF) promote weight loss but risk significant muscle loss, posing health implications to seniors at risk of sarcopenia. Leucine, the key muscle protein synthesis (MPS) driver, effectively stimulates MPS with lower calorie intake than protein. However, the effects of body-mass-scaled protein and leucine intakes are unclear. Objectives: To evaluate body-mass-scaled leucine or protein supplementation on body composition, sarcopenic, and cardiometabolic markers in older men during ADF. Methods: Sixty-one older men (BMI ≥ 23.0 kg/m2) underwent 28 days of ADF, randomized across three calorie-matched supplement groups: Control (C: 0.0 g/kg protein, 0.0 g/kg leucine), Leucine (L: 0.0 g/kg protein, 0.08 g/kg leucine), or Protein (P: 0.4 g/kg protein, 0.04 g/kg leucine), consuming three doses on feeding days and one on fasting days. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, sarcopenic metrics, and blood markers (blood pressure, lipid panels, diabetic profiles) were measured. Results: There were no significant interactions (p > 0.05) in body composition, sarcopenic or health outcomes, except for diastolic blood pressure (p = 0.016) and HDL cholesterol (p = 0.013). There were significant main effects of time (p ≤ 0.05) with reductions in all body composition measures (excluding bone mineral density, p = 0.274), systolic blood pressure and lipid profiles (total and LDL cholesterol, total/HDL cholesterol ratio, triglycerides), and improvements in all muscle strength and functional sarcopenic outcomes. Conclusions: Dietary interventions alone that increase leucine and/or protein intake did not result in additional measurable improvements during this four-week intervention on body composition, sarcopenic, and cardiometabolic outcomes during weight loss.

items.title: Effects of Probiotic Supplementation on Performance Retention During Detraining and Recovery After Simulated Return-to-Training Stress in College Volleyball Players: An Exploratory Randomized, Single-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial.
items.abstract: Background: The effects of probiotic supplementation on performance and recovery during training transitions remain uncertain. This exploratory trial examined the effects of probiotic supplementation on performance, recovery, and gut microbiota in national-level university volleyball players. Methods: Twenty-eight players were randomized to receive a multi-strain probiotic or placebo (n = 14 per group) for 8 weeks, comprising regular training, tapering and competition, and reduced training. Performance and gut microbiota were assessed before and after supplementation. Participants then completed 200 weighted vertical jumps as a simulated return-to-training stressor, with recovery monitored for 48 h. Results: Before accounting for multiple comparisons, the probiotic group showed smaller declines in shuttle-test performance and standing and approach vertical jump height across the intervention period, with no significant between-group differences in maximal-strength or Wingate outcomes. Following the simulated return-to-training stressor, the probiotic group showed lower muscle soreness and creatine kinase responses and smaller reductions in selected strength-recovery and rate-of-force-development measures. After accounting for multiple comparisons, only lower muscle soreness and a smaller reduction in non-dominant knee extension maximum work at 180°/s at 24 h remained significant. Chao1 richness decreased more in the probiotic group, whereas changes in Simpson diversity and the relative abundances of Firmicutes, Lachnospiraceae, and Bifidobacteriaceae did not differ between groups. Conclusions: Eight weeks of multi-strain probiotic supplementation was associated with selected differences in performance and recovery during a training transition. However, after accounting for multiple comparisons, the evidence was limited to lower muscle soreness and a smaller reduction in non-dominant knee extension maximum work at 24 h. These exploratory findings require confirmation in larger, prospectively registered trials with prespecified outcomes.

items.title: A Randomized Clinical Trial of a Standardized Pumpkin-Seed-Derived Peptide Extract: Body Composition Outcomes and Exploratory Analysis by Baseline Adiposity in Overweight Adults.
items.abstract: This 12-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 50 overweight adults who received either a standardized pumpkin-seed-derived preparation (IRK-19®, 600 mg/day) or placebo. The clinical preparation contained 66.2% crude protein; components with apparent molecular weights ≤6.29 kDa accounted for 23.6% of the total SEC-UV chromatographic area, and the combined HPLC-measured content of six selected peptide markers was 2.79% (w/w). Among the 48 participants with evaluable DXA data at Week 12, between-group comparisons of body weight, BMI, and adiposity-related outcomes did not reach statistical significance in the overall study population. In a post hoc exploratory subgroup defined by baseline total fat mass ≥28.4 kg (the study-specific 75th percentile; n = 13), adjusted between-group differences (IRK-19® minus placebo) at Week 12 were -2.30 kg for body weight (95% CI, -4.08 to -0.51; p = 0.018), -0.75 kg/m2 for BMI (95% CI, -1.48 to -0.02; p = 0.045), and -1.60 kg for total fat mass (95% CI, -3.23 to 0.04; p = 0.055). Treatment-by-baseline-fat-mass interactions did not reach statistical significance for body weight, BMI, or total fat mass (p = 0.065, 0.106, and 0.057, respectively). These post hoc subgroup findings warrant further investigation but were not adjusted for multiple comparisons. Prospectively designed trials with prespecified adiposity strata are needed to determine whether baseline fat mass is associated with differential treatment response.
